lead: OpenAI fires three safety researchers who had urged labs to slow down, days before trimming its revenue story by $20B; Brad Smith says milk is more regulated than AI; and Karpathy maps a widening funnel between the 20 million who see what agents do and everyone else.

sections.title: OpenAI, safety and the revenue story
sections.intro: Three fired researchers, an outside auditor, and a $20B correction.

sections.title: Rules, branding and who sets them
sections.intro: Regulation calls from Microsoft, a Palantir defense, and the super intelligence rebrand.

sections.title: How to think about the transition
sections.intro: Essays and tools for reasoning about where AI goes next.

sections.title: Deals and builds
sections.intro: An Amazon-Decart talk, hospital staffing money, a sandbox for agent code, and routers.

sections.title: Does the money add up
sections.intro: An IPO bear case, a productivity reality check, and a supercycle bet.

sections.title: Built with AI, measured carefully
sections.intro: What agents ship, and how we check what they ship.

sections.title: Energy, access and other paths
sections.intro: China's grid bet, restored safety access, and a non-LLM road.

sections.title: The safety debate sharpens
sections.intro: A day of open conflict over how frontier AI should be governed: OpenAI publicly answered the three departed safety researchers, Anthropic detailed unintended model actions it caught in its own evaluations, and Microsoft's Satya Nadella called for an emergency brake humans control - while Brad Smith warned AI is less regulated than milk, and the question of who pays the independent evaluators got harder to ignore.

sections.title: Chips, capital and the AI build-out
sections.intro: Microsoft unveiled its third-generation Maia 300 inference chip while the money side of the boom took center stage: Broadcom's and Intel's CEOs warned capital - not chips or power - may be the binding constraint, Hock Tan likened uninformed AI investors to casino gamblers, and Tencent lined up a $5 billion bond mostly for chip purchases as Nvidia reportedly eyed a bigger Reflection stake.

sections.title: New models, and how they actually work
sections.intro: Clef-omni arrived with full multimodality alongside faster and cheaper siblings, Microsoft introduced Decision-1 for fast decision-making, and Google's Gemini 4 Argon hints surfaced through checkpoint testing - while a first-principles derivation of speculative decoding explained why the trick of checking several tokens for the price of one works at all.

sections.title: Agents, tooling and the engineering workflow
sections.intro: A case study asked whether agent teams actually pay off on real coding tasks, Anthropic opened Claude Code Projects to every Pro and Max user, and QGIS drew a hard line by banning AI-assisted contributions - a snapshot of a profession negotiating where AI fits inside its own tools.

sections.title: Work, labor and the backlash
sections.intro: Cory Doctorow told how labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist, the New York Times documented a human 'verification tax' eating AI's promised efficiency gains, and Sean Goedecke argued software engineers - the people who build the automation machine - don't get to be Luddites about it, as anti-AI anger turns increasingly physical.

sections.title: Meta's Wonder, and what it takes to power it
sections.intro: Meta launches Muse Wonder as Microsoft and Bloomberg put numbers on the hardware behind the race.

sections.title: Agents get orchestrated, sandboxed and questioned
sections.intro: Anthropic's flows, cheap sandboxes and reverse-engineering agents, alongside worries about what agents install and do.

sections.title: Self-replication, scams and the case for saying no
sections.intro: A new Anthropic red-team study on self-copying models sits next to scams, hacking and policy pushback.
